chunks: High-side NFET vs PFET trade-offs. The question: NFET vs PFET for high-side FET? What are pros and cons?
An NFET is the better transistor: for the same size it has lower resistance. A PFET is easier to drive on the high side. The trade-off is simple.
The NFET needs a gate voltage higher than the input, which takes extra circuitry, and the PFET does not but is bigger and loses more.
Imagine a button on a floating raft that rises and falls with the tide. To press it you need a finger that rises with the raft, so you must carry your own platform.
That is the NFET on the high side, whose source moves with the switch node. A PFET is like a button fixed to the dock, easy to reach but of poorer quality.
The PFET's source is tied to V in . R pu holds the gate at V in (off). When the small NFET Q LS turns on it pulls the gate toward ground through R g , giving V GS about -V in .
Because V GS is limited (usually 20 volts), above that you add a Zener clamp or a divider. The freewheel element here is a diode, but a low-side NFET works the same way.
NFET / PFET: N-type and P-type MOSFETs; the N-type has lower resistance for its size.
Gate-source voltage ( V GS ): the voltage between gate and source that turns the transistor on.
Bootstrap: a capacitor trick that lifts the gate above the input ("Design a high-side NFET drive"). R DS(on) : the transistor's resistance when fully on.
100 percent duty: holding the switch on all the time, possible with a PFET.
Take a 12 volts input. A PFET has its source at 12 volts, so pulling its gate down to about 7 volts turns it on, and 12 volts turns it off.
An NFET, once on, has its source up near 12 volts too, so its gate must reach about 12 plus 5 equals 17 volts. That is above any supply on the board, so a bootstrap is needed.
"An NFET is the better switch and a PFET is the easier one to drive.

NFETs have two to three times lower R DS(on) per area because electrons are more mobile than holes, so less gate charge and capacitance and lower cost, but a high-side NFET needs its gate above V in , so a bootstrap or charge pump, and it can't reach 100% duty without refresh.
A high-side PFET just pulls its gate down relative to V in and supports 100% duty, at the cost of larger die, more switching loss and slower edges.
PFET for low voltage and simplicity, NFET for efficiency and current."
